title: Neurons, nerves and the resting potential

course.unit: Lab 1 · Nerve physiology, reflexes & general senses

summary: What a neuron and a nerve are, and why the inside of a resting cell sits at about -70 mV.
objectives: Name the three parts of a neuron and say what a nerve is made of
State the resting membrane potential and explain why K+ sets it
Predict what raising extracellular K+ or Na+ does to the resting potential
Explain the job of the Na+/K+ pump and what ouabain does to it
takeaways: Dendrites receive, the cell body integrates, the axon conducts; a nerve is a bundle of axons wrapped in connective tissue.
A resting neuron is about -70 mV inside, close to the K+ equilibrium potential because K+ leak channels dominate at rest.
Raising extracellular K+ depolarises the cell; changing extracellular Na+ barely moves the resting potential.
The Na+/K+ ATPase (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in) maintains the gradients; ouabain blocks it and the gradients slowly run down.

steps.title: Three parts of a neuron
steps.text:
A neuron has dendrites that receive signals, a cell body (soma) holding the nucleus that adds those signals up, and a single axon that carries the output away. The axon begins at the axon hillock, the trigger zone, and ends in terminals that release neurotransmitter onto the next cell.

Information therefore flows one way: dendrite, cell body, axon, terminal.

The neuron model shows the whole cell, from dendrites to the boutons of the axon terminals.

check.q: Which part of a neuron conducts the signal away from the cell body?
check.a: The axon, starting at the axon hillock and ending at the axon terminals.

steps.title: A nerve is a cable of axons
steps.text: A nerve is not one cell: it is a bundle of many axons running together outside the brain and spinal cord. The sciatic nerve in the back of the thigh holds thousands of them. In the micro model each axon sits in its own endoneurium, bundles are wrapped in perineurium, and the whole nerve in epineurium. Many axons are wrapped in myelin; the gaps between wraps are the nodes of Ranvier.

check.q: Where are the cell bodies of the axons in the sciatic nerve?
check.a: Not in the nerve: motor cell bodies lie in the spinal cord's anterior horn and sensory ones in the dorsal root ganglia. A nerve holds only their axons.

steps.title: The resting membrane potential
steps.text:
Push a fine glass microelectrode through a cell membrane and the inside reads negative: about -70 mV in a neuron and a little more negative in skeletal muscle fibres. That voltage is the resting membrane potential (RMP).

It exists because ions are unevenly spread. Outside there is about 145 mEq/L of Na+ and 5 mEq/L of K+; inside it is roughly the reverse, about 140 mEq/L of K+ and 15 mEq/L of Na+. (mEq/L counts charges per litre.)

check.q: Which ion is concentrated inside the cell and which outside?
check.a: K+ is high inside (about 140 mEq/L); Na+ is high outside (about 145 mEq/L).

steps.title: Why potassium sets the voltage
steps.text:
At rest the membrane has many open K+ leak channels and very few open Na+ channels. K+ leaks out down its gradient, leaving negative charge behind, until the inside is negative enough to hold it back: the K+ equilibrium potential (about -90 mV), which the Nernst equation calculates from the concentration ratio. Na+ has its own equilibrium potential, about +60 mV, but its low permeability lets it pull the RMP up only slightly.

So raising extracellular K+ makes the RMP less negative (depolarised); changing extracellular Na+ barely moves it.
steps.clinical: Hyperkalaemia (high blood K+) depolarises heart and nerve cells and can cause dangerous arrhythmias, which is why potassium levels are watched so closely.

check.q: Extracellular K+ is raised from 5 to 20 mEq/L. What happens to the resting potential, and why?
check.a: It becomes less negative (depolarises), because the K+ gradient that sets the RMP is smaller.

steps.title: The Na+/K+ pump keeps the gradients
steps.text:
Leaks would slowly flatten both gradients. The Na+/K+ ATPase prevents that: each cycle uses one ATP to push 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in. It maintains the concentration differences that the RMP depends on (and adds a few millivolts itself).

Ouabain blocks the pump. The RMP does not collapse at once; it drifts toward zero over minutes as the gradients run down.
steps.pitfall: The pump is not what makes the moment-to-moment resting voltage; K+ leak does. Block the pump and the potential fades slowly, not instantly.

check.q: What does ouabain do, and how quickly does the resting potential change afterwards?
check.a: It blocks the Na+/K+ ATPase; the RMP becomes less negative gradually as the ion gradients run down.

practice.q: Put the parts of a neuron in the order a signal passes through them
The resting membrane potential of a typical neuron is about
practice.why: The inside is negative at rest, about -70 mV, near the K+ equilibrium potential.

practice.q: Which ion's movement mainly determines the resting potential?
practice.why: At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K+ than to any other ion.

practice.q: Raising extracellular K+ makes the resting potential
practice.why: A smaller K+ gradient means less K+ leaves, so less negative charge is left inside.

practice.q: Doubling extracellular Na+ changes the resting potential
practice.why: Few Na+ channels are open at rest, so Na+ has little influence on the RMP.

practice.q: What does the Nernst equation give you?
practice.a: The equilibrium potential of one ion: the voltage at which its electrical and concentration forces balance (about -90 mV for K+, +60 mV for Na+).

practice.q: What does the Na+/K+ ATPase move per cycle, and which drug blocks it?
practice.a: 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in for one ATP; ouabain blocks it.

practice.q: What unit is used for ion concentrations in body fluids, and what does it count?
practice.a: mEq/L (milliequivalents per litre) - the amount of charge carried by the ions per litre.

practice.q: How is the membrane potential of a single cell measured?
practice.a: With an intracellular microelectrode inside the cell compared with a reference electrode outside.

title: EPSPs, IPSPs and summation

course.unit: Lab 1 · Nerve physiology, reflexes & general senses

summary: Small graded potentials at synapses, and how a neuron adds them up to decide whether to fire.
objectives: Define EPSP, IPSP and graded potential
Explain why graded potentials fade with time and distance
Distinguish temporal from spatial summation
Say where summation decides whether an action potential fires
takeaways: An EPSP is a small graded depolarisation at a synapse; an IPSP is a small graded hyperpolarisation.
Graded potentials vary with stimulus strength and die away with time and distance.
Temporal summation: repeated inputs close together in time add - the shorter the interval, the bigger the sum.
Spatial summation: inputs from different synapses arriving together add; an EPSP and an IPSP can cancel.
If the summed potential at the axon hillock reaches threshold, an action potential fires.

steps.title: Synapses make graded potentials
steps.text:
At a chemical synapse, transmitter from one neuron opens ion channels on the next. If the channels let positive ions in, the membrane depolarises a little: an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP). If they let K+ out or Cl- in, it hyperpolarises: an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP).

Both are graded potentials: their size depends on how much transmitter arrives, unlike the fixed-size action potential.

check.q: Is an IPSP a depolarisation or a hyperpolarisation?
check.a: A hyperpolarisation - it moves the membrane further from threshold.

steps.title: Graded potentials fade
steps.text: A graded potential spreads passively from the synapse, like ripples from a stone. Charge leaks out across the membrane as it goes, so the potential shrinks with distance and dies away within milliseconds. A single EPSP on a distant dendrite is usually far too small to matter by the time it reaches the axon hillock, where the neuron's trigger zone sits.
steps.pitfall: The neuromuscular junction is the exception: its end-plate potential is so large that one nerve impulse always fires the muscle fibre. Neuron-to-neuron synapses need summation.

check.q: Name two ways a graded potential differs from an action potential.
check.a: It varies in size with the stimulus, and it decays with time and distance instead of travelling unchanged along the axon.

steps.title: Temporal summation
steps.text:
If one synapse fires again before its first EPSP has died away, the second EPSP starts from a raised baseline and the two add. That is temporal summation - summation in time.

The shorter the interval between stimuli, the less each EPSP has decayed and the larger the summed EPSP. A fast enough train can carry the membrane to threshold even though each EPSP alone is small.

check.q: Two stimuli are given 5 ms apart, then 20 ms apart. Which gives the larger summed EPSP?
check.a: 5 ms apart - the first EPSP has decayed less when the second arrives.

steps.title: Spatial summation and cancellation
steps.text:
A motor neuron in the anterior horn receives thousands of synapses. EPSPs from different synapses at the same moment add together: spatial summation.

Excitation and inhibition are summed too: an EPSP and an IPSP of equal size arriving together cancel. The neuron fires only if the net potential at the axon hillock reaches threshold - so every cell is constantly weighing its inputs.

On the neuron model, find the axon hillock where the cell body narrows into the axon.

check.q: An EPSP and an equal IPSP arrive at the same time. What happens?
check.a: They cancel, leaving the membrane near rest; no action potential is triggered.

practice.q: An EPSP is
practice.why: Excitatory postsynaptic potentials move the membrane toward threshold.

practice.q: An IPSP makes a neuron
practice.why: It hyperpolarises the membrane, moving it away from threshold.

practice.q: Repeated stimuli at one synapse, close together in time, add up. This is
practice.why: Temporal = same synapse, successive inputs in time.

practice.q: Several different synapses fire at the same moment and their EPSPs add. This is
practice.why: Spatial = different locations at the same time.

practice.q: Shortening the interval between two stimuli makes the summed EPSP
practice.why: Less time for the first EPSP to decay before the second adds to it.

practice.q: Why do graded potentials not travel far?
practice.a: They spread passively and leak charge across the membrane, so they shrink with distance and decay with time.

practice.q: Where on a neuron is the summed potential compared with threshold?
practice.a: At the axon hillock (the trigger zone), where the axon leaves the cell body.

title: Action potentials and refractory periods

course.unit: Lab 1 · Nerve physiology, reflexes & general senses

summary: The all-or-none spike of one axon, the refractory periods that follow it, and the compound action potential of a whole nerve.
objectives: Link each phase of the action potential to the voltage-gated channel responsible
Explain threshold and the all-or-none principle
Distinguish the absolute and relative refractory periods
Explain why a compound action potential grows with stimulus intensity
takeaways: Depolarisation: voltage-gated Na+ channels open. Repolarisation: Na+ channels inactivate and voltage-gated K+ channels open. The slow K+ close gives an undershoot (hyperpolarisation).
A single axon fires a full-size action potential once threshold is reached, or none at all.
Absolute refractory period: no second spike at any strength. Relative: a second spike needs a stronger stimulus.
A nerve's compound action potential is the sum of many axons' spikes, so it grows from threshold to maximal stimulus as more axons are recruited.

steps.title: The spike and its channels
steps.text:
When the axon hillock reaches threshold (about -55 mV), voltage-gated Na+ channels open and Na+ rushes in: depolarisation, overshooting to about +30 mV. Within a millisecond the Na+ channels inactivate and slower voltage-gated K+ channels open, letting K+ out: repolarisation. The K+ channels are slow to close, so the membrane briefly dips below rest: hyperpolarisation, the undershoot.

The neuron model's view “Sodium channels at the node” shows such channels clustered at a node of Ranvier.
micro_focus: Node detail: NaV1.6 channel 1, α subunit
Node detail: NaV1.6 channel 2, α subunit
Node detail: NaV1.6 channel 3, α subunit
Node detail: axon membrane at the node

check.q: Which channel opening causes the rising phase, and which the falling phase?
check.a: Voltage-gated Na+ channels (Na+ in) for depolarisation; voltage-gated K+ channels (K+ out) for repolarisation.

steps.title: Threshold and all-or-none
steps.text:
Below threshold a stimulus gives only a local graded potential that fades. At threshold, opening Na+ channels depolarise the membrane, which opens more Na+ channels - a self-feeding loop that always runs to the same peak. A single axon therefore obeys the all-or-none principle: a full action potential or none.

A stronger stimulus does not make a bigger spike; it makes spikes more frequent.

check.q: How does a single axon signal a stronger stimulus?
check.a: By firing action potentials more often; each spike stays the same size (all-or-none).

steps.title: Refractory periods
steps.text:
During the spike and most of repolarisation the Na+ channels are open or inactivated, so no stimulus, however strong, can start a second one: the absolute refractory period. Next comes the relative refractory period: some Na+ channels have reset but K+ is still flowing out, so a second spike needs a stronger-than-threshold stimulus.

Refractory periods cap the firing rate and stop impulses running backwards.

check.q: A second stimulus of threshold strength arrives during the relative refractory period. Does it fire?
check.a: No - during the relative refractory period a stronger-than-threshold stimulus is needed.

steps.title: The compound action potential
steps.text:
Record from a whole nerve and you see a compound action potential (CAP): the summed spikes of all the axons that fired. Axons differ in threshold (large ones fire first), so the CAP is graded. At the threshold stimulus the first axons fire; raising stimulus intensity recruits more, until at the maximal stimulus every axon fires and the CAP stops growing.

Give two stimuli very close together and the second CAP is smaller or absent: many axons are still refractory.
steps.pitfall: A single axon is all-or-none, but a whole nerve is not - its CAP grows with the stimulus because more axons join in.

check.q: Why does a nerve's CAP get bigger as stimulus voltage rises, when each axon is all-or-none?
check.a: More axons with higher thresholds are recruited, and the CAP is the sum of all their spikes.

practice.q: The rising (depolarising) phase of the action potential is caused by
practice.why: Na+ rushes in through voltage-gated Na+ channels once threshold is reached.

practice.q: The undershoot after an action potential is due to
practice.why: K+ keeps leaving for a moment after the membrane has returned to rest.

practice.q: During the absolute refractory period
choices: no stimulus can trigger a second action potential
a stronger stimulus can trigger a second action potential
practice.why: Na+ channels are open or inactivated, so they cannot reopen.

practice.q: A compound action potential grows with stimulus voltage because
practice.why: Each axon is all-or-none; the nerve's response is the sum of the axons that fire.

practice.q: Two stimuli are given 1 ms apart to a nerve. The second CAP is
practice.why: Most axons are still in their refractory period.

practice.q: State the all-or-none principle.
practice.a: Once threshold is reached an axon fires a full-size action potential; below threshold it fires none.

practice.q: Distinguish threshold stimulus from maximal stimulus for a nerve.
practice.a: Threshold: the weakest stimulus that makes any axon fire (the first visible CAP). Maximal: the weakest that makes every axon fire, so the CAP is as large as it can be.

practice.q: Put the phases of an action potential in order

title: Fibre classes and what excites a nerve

course.unit: Lab 1 · Nerve physiology, reflexes & general senses

summary: Why thick myelinated fibres conduct fastest, and how a nerve-muscle preparation shows threshold, recruitment and the effects of chemicals, temperature and local anaesthetic.
objectives: Classify nerve fibres as A, B or C by diameter, myelin and speed
Explain saltatory conduction
Define threshold voltage and maximum recruitment voltage in a nerve-muscle preparation
List the kinds of stimulus that excite a nerve and explain how procaine and cold block conduction
takeaways: A fibres: thick, heavily myelinated, fastest. B: thinner, lightly myelinated. C: thinnest, unmyelinated, slowest.
Conduction velocity rises with axon diameter and with myelination; myelinated axons conduct by saltatory conduction.
Threshold voltage gives the first visible twitch; maximum recruitment voltage stimulates every axon and gives the biggest twitch.
Nerves respond to mechanical, electrical, chemical and thermal stimuli.
Procaine (Novocain) reversibly blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels; cold slows and eventually blocks conduction.

steps.title: A, B and C fibres
steps.text:
Nerve fibres are classed by fibre diameter and myelination, which together set conduction velocity. A fibres are thick and heavily myelinated - up to about 120 m/s (motor to skeletal muscle, touch, proprioception). B fibres are thinner and lightly myelinated (preganglionic autonomic). C fibres are thin and unmyelinated, about 1 m/s (slow pain, temperature, postganglionic autonomic).

In myelinated axons the impulse jumps from node to node: saltatory conduction.

check.q: Which two features of an axon increase its conduction velocity?
check.a: A larger diameter and myelination (which allows saltatory conduction).

steps.title: The nerve-muscle preparation
steps.text:
The classic model is the frog's sciatic nerve, which leaves the sacral region, runs down the posterior thigh and supplies the gastrocnemius. The frog is doubly pithed (brain and spinal cord destroyed) so it feels nothing and has no reflexes, and the tissue is kept moist with Ringer's solution, a physiological saline.

An impulse in the nerve crosses the neuromuscular junction, and the muscle gives a brief contraction - a twitch - pulling on the calcaneal tendon. The human arrangement is the same.

check.q: Why is Ringer's solution used on an isolated nerve?
check.a: It is a physiological salt solution that keeps the nerve and muscle alive and excitable.

steps.title: Threshold and maximum recruitment voltage
steps.text:
Stimulate the nerve with rising voltages. The threshold voltage is the lowest that produces a visible twitch - the first axons have fired. Higher voltages recruit more axons, so more muscle fibres contract and the twitch grows. At the maximum recruitment voltage every axon in the nerve fires and the twitch is as strong as it gets; more voltage adds nothing.

This is the compound action potential again, read out as force.

check.q: Why does the twitch stop growing above the maximum recruitment voltage?
check.a: All the axons in the nerve are already firing, so no more muscle fibres can be recruited.

steps.title: Many kinds of stimulus
steps.text:
Electricity is not the only thing that fires a nerve. Mechanical stimuli - a pinch, or tying a thread tightly around it (ligation) - trigger impulses. Chemical stimuli such as hydrochloric acid or strong (hypertonic) sodium chloride do too. Heat stimulates a nerve and, if strong, damages it.

Anything that depolarises the axon to threshold starts an action potential; damaging stimuli may fire it once and then destroy its ability to conduct.

check.q: Name four types of stimulus that can excite a nerve.
check.a: Mechanical (pinch, ligation), electrical, chemical (HCl, hypertonic NaCl) and thermal (heat).

steps.title: Blocking conduction: anaesthetic and cold
steps.text:
Procaine hydrochloride (Novocain) is a local anaesthetic. It blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels, so action potentials cannot pass the treated segment. The block is reversible: after a recovery time as the drug washes away, conduction returns.

Cold slows channel gating, so conduction slows and, if cold enough, stops - also reversibly. Thin, unmyelinated pain fibres are blocked most easily.
steps.clinical: Dentists and surgeons inject local anaesthetics near a nerve (a nerve block). Pain goes first and pressure sense and movement last, because small fibres are blocked first.

check.q: How does procaine stop a nerve conducting, and is the effect permanent?
check.a: It blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels; the effect wears off after a recovery time.

practice.q: Which fibres conduct fastest?
choices: All conduct at the same speed
practice.why: Diameter and myelin both raise conduction velocity.

practice.q: Slow burning pain travels mainly in
practice.why: C fibres are thin and unmyelinated, conducting about 0.5-2 m/s.

practice.q: Saltatory conduction means the impulse
practice.why: Myelin insulates the internodes, so depolarisation regenerates only at the nodes of Ranvier.

practice.q: The lowest voltage that produces a visible muscle twitch is the
practice.why: It is the first voltage that fires any axons in the nerve.

practice.q: Procaine (Novocain) blocks nerve conduction by
practice.why: Without Na+ entry the axon cannot depolarise; the block wears off with time.

practice.q: What does 'doubly pithed' mean, and why is it done?
practice.a: Both brain and spinal cord are destroyed, so the animal feels no pain and has no reflexes, leaving nerve and muscle intact.

practice.q: What happens to nerve conduction when the nerve is cooled?
practice.a: It slows and, if cold enough, is blocked - reversibly on rewarming.

practice.q: What is a twitch?
practice.a: A single brief contraction of a muscle in response to one stimulus.

title: The reflex arc

course.unit: Lab 1 · Nerve physiology, reflexes & general senses

summary: Five parts, two roots and one decision point: how a reflex is wired, and how reflexes are graded in the clinic.
objectives: Define a reflex and name the five components of a reflex arc
Trace the arc through the dorsal root ganglion, dorsal root, grey matter, ventral root and spinal nerve
Distinguish somatic from visceral reflexes and monosynaptic from polysynaptic arcs
Grade reflexes and relate hypo- and hyperreflexia to their causes
takeaways: A reflex is a rapid, involuntary, predictable motor response to a stimulus.
Receptor -> sensory (afferent) neuron -> integration centre -> motor (efferent) neuron -> effector.
Sensory cell bodies sit in the dorsal root ganglion; motor axons leave by the ventral root; both run in the spinal nerve.
Somatic reflexes move skeletal muscle; visceral (autonomic) reflexes act on smooth muscle, cardiac muscle or glands.
Hyporeflexia suggests peripheral nerve damage or hypothyroidism; hyperreflexia suggests CNS (upper motor neuron) damage. Always compare sides.

steps.title: What a reflex is
steps.text: A reflex is a rapid, involuntary and predictable motor response to a stimulus, produced without conscious thought. Its pathway, the reflex arc, has five parts: a receptor that detects the stimulus, an afferent (sensory) neuron, an integration centre in the brain or spinal cord, an efferent (motor) neuron, and an effector that responds.

check.q: List the five components of a reflex arc in order.
check.a: Receptor, sensory (afferent) neuron, integration centre, motor (efferent) neuron, effector.

steps.title: The route through the cord
steps.text:
The sensory neuron's cell body lies in the dorsal root ganglion; its axon enters the cord through the dorsal root into the posterior horn of the grey matter. The motor neuron's cell body sits in the anterior horn, and its axon leaves by the ventral root. The two roots join as the spinal nerve, which carries both.

Branches also climb the white matter in ascending tracts, so the brain learns what happened - after the reflex has already acted.

check.q: Where are the cell bodies of the sensory and motor neurons of a spinal reflex?
check.a: Sensory: dorsal root ganglion. Motor: anterior (ventral) horn of the spinal cord grey matter.

steps.title: Somatic and visceral reflexes
steps.text: Reflexes are named by their effector. Somatic reflexes act on skeletal muscle - withdrawing a hand from a hot pan, or the knee-jerk. Visceral (autonomic) reflexes act on smooth muscle, cardiac muscle or glands - the pupil narrowing in bright light, salivating at the smell of food, or the heart slowing when blood pressure rises.

check.q: The pupil constricts in bright light. Is this a somatic or a visceral reflex?
check.a: Visceral (autonomic) - its effector is smooth muscle of the iris.

steps.title: Monosynaptic and polysynaptic arcs
steps.text:
In a monosynaptic reflex arc the sensory neuron synapses directly on the motor neuron - one synapse, very fast. The stretch reflex is the classic example.

A polysynaptic reflex arc has one or more interneurons between them, so there are several synapses. It is slower but can do more: withdrawal from pain bends one limb while straightening the other and involves several spinal segments.

check.q: What cell does a polysynaptic reflex have that a monosynaptic one lacks?
check.a: At least one interneuron between the sensory and motor neurons.

steps.title: Grading reflexes
steps.text:
Reflexes are tested with a reflex hammer and described as normal, hyporeflexic (depressed or absent) or hyperreflexic (exaggerated). Depressed reflexes follow damage to the peripheral nerve or the reflex arc itself, and occur in hypothyroidism. Exaggerated reflexes follow CNS damage to descending (upper motor neuron) pathways, which normally damp the arc.

Always compare left with right: reflexes should be symmetrical.
steps.clinical: An asymmetric reflex matters more than a uniformly brisk or sluggish set: one hyperreflexic side points to a lesion in the opposite brain hemisphere or the same side of the cord.

check.q: Brisk, exaggerated reflexes suggest damage where?
check.a: In the CNS - the upper motor neuron (descending) pathways that normally inhibit the reflex arc.

The cell bodies of sensory neurons in a spinal reflex lie in the
practice.why: The dorsal root ganglion is the swelling on the dorsal root.

practice.q: A reflex whose effector is a gland or smooth muscle is
practice.why: Somatic reflexes act on skeletal muscle only.

practice.q: A monosynaptic reflex arc has
choices: one synapse, between sensory and motor neuron
its synapse in the dorsal root ganglion
practice.why: The stretch reflex is the classic monosynaptic arc.

practice.q: Depressed reflexes are expected in
practice.why: Hypothyroidism and peripheral nerve damage give hyporeflexia; CNS damage gives hyperreflexia.

practice.q: Define a reflex.
practice.a: A rapid, involuntary, predictable motor response to a stimulus, occurring without conscious thought.

practice.q: How does the brain find out about a spinal reflex?
practice.a: Sensory branches also synapse on neurons whose axons ascend in the white-matter tracts to the brain.

title: Stretch reflexes: knee, elbow and ankle

course.unit: Lab 1 · Nerve physiology, reflexes & general senses

summary: The muscle spindle and the four deep tendon reflexes: where to tap, what moves, which nerve and which cord segments.
objectives: Explain how the muscle spindle drives a monosynaptic stretch reflex
For the patellar, biceps, triceps and calcaneal reflexes, give the tendon tapped, the movement, the nerve and the spinal segments
Find each tendon, muscle and nerve in the 3D atlas
takeaways: Tapping a tendon stretches its muscle; spindles fire and the same muscle contracts by a monosynaptic arc.
Patellar: patellar ligament, quadriceps, knee extends, femoral nerve, L2-L4.
Biceps: thumb over the tendon in the cubital fossa, elbow flexes, musculocutaneous nerve, C5-C6.
Triceps: tendon just above the olecranon, elbow extends, radial nerve, C6-C8.
Calcaneal (Achilles): calcaneal tendon, plantar flexion by gastrocnemius and soleus, tibial nerve, S1-S2.

steps.title: The muscle spindle
steps.text:
Inside every skeletal muscle lie muscle spindles: a few thin intrafusal fibres in a capsule, wrapped by sensory endings. They are stretch receptors. Stretch the muscle and the spindle fires; its sensory axon synapses directly on motor neurons to the same muscle, which contracts and resists the stretch.

This stretch reflex is monosynaptic. Tapping a tendon with a reflex hammer gives a quick stretch, which is why these are also called deep tendon reflexes.

check.q: In a stretch reflex, which muscle contracts?
check.a: The muscle that was stretched - its own spindles excite its own motor neurons.

steps.title: The patellar (knee-jerk) reflex
steps.text: Tap the patellar ligament just below the patella. The quadriceps femoris is stretched, its spindles fire, and it contracts: the knee extends and the leg kicks forward. The arc runs in the femoral nerve through spinal segments L2-L4.

check.q: Which nerve and spinal segments carry the patellar reflex?
check.a: The femoral nerve, segments L2-L4.

steps.title: Biceps and triceps reflexes
steps.text:
Biceps: with the elbow bent, put your thumb on the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa and tap the thumb. The biceps brachii contracts and the elbow flexes. Nerve: musculocutaneous, segments C5-C6.

Triceps: tap the triceps tendon just above the olecranon. The triceps brachii contracts and the elbow extends. Nerve: radial, segments C6-C8.

check.q: Tapping just above the olecranon extends the elbow. Which nerve carries this reflex?
check.a: The radial nerve (triceps reflex, C6-C8).

steps.title: The calcaneal (Achilles) reflex
steps.text:
Tap the calcaneal tendon behind the ankle. The gastrocnemius and soleus contract and the foot plantar flexes - points downward. The arc runs in the tibial nerve, segments S1-S2.

Very well-developed muscles can make a normal reflex look small, so judge the response against the other side, not against an ideal.
steps.clinical: An absent ankle jerk with normal knee jerks is a common sign of an S1 root lesion, typically from an L5-S1 disc prolapse.

check.q: What movement does the calcaneal reflex produce, and which muscles do it?
check.a: Plantar flexion of the foot, by gastrocnemius and soleus.

practice.q: The receptor for a stretch reflex is the
practice.why: Spindles are stretch receptors lying among the muscle fibres.

practice.q: The patellar reflex tests spinal segments
practice.why: Femoral nerve, L2-L4.

practice.q: The biceps reflex is carried by the
practice.why: Musculocutaneous nerve, C5-C6.

practice.q: Tapping the calcaneal tendon causes
practice.why: Gastrocnemius and soleus contract via the tibial nerve (S1-S2).

practice.q: Why is the stretch reflex called monosynaptic?
practice.a: The spindle's sensory neuron synapses directly on the motor neuron - one synapse, no interneuron.

title: Blink, corneal and plantar reflexes

course.unit: Lab 1 · Nerve physiology, reflexes & general senses

summary: Two reflexes that protect the eye and one on the sole of the foot that reveals damage to the corticospinal tracts.
objectives: Distinguish the blink (menace) reflex from the corneal reflex
Name the afferent and efferent nerves of the corneal reflex
Describe the normal plantar response and the Babinski sign, and explain what a Babinski sign means in an adult and in an infant
takeaways: Blink reflex to a threat protects the cornea and can be partly suppressed; the corneal reflex cannot be suppressed.
Corneal reflex: touch the cornea -> both eyes blink. In via the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal (V1), out via the facial nerve (VII) to orbicularis oculi.
Stroke the lateral sole from heel to ball of foot: adults normally flex (curl) the toes.
Babinski sign: the big toe extends and the others fan - normal under about 1 year (corticospinal tracts not fully myelinated), a sign of corticospinal tract damage in adults.

steps.title: The blink reflex
steps.text: A hand flicked toward your face makes you blink: the blink reflex (menace or threat reflex). It protects the cornea, the clear front window of the eye, by sweeping the eyelids shut. Because this reflex passes through the brain's visual system, you can learn to suppress it partly - try not to blink and you often succeed.

check.q: What does the blink reflex protect, and can it be voluntarily suppressed?
check.a: The cornea; yes, it can be partly suppressed.

steps.title: The corneal reflex
steps.text:
Touch the cornea, or puff air on it, and both eyes blink at once - the corneal reflex. The cornea is densely supplied by free nerve endings of the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve (afferent). The motor side is the facial nerve (VII) to orbicularis oculi (efferent).

Unlike the menace blink, it cannot be inhibited voluntarily.
steps.clinical: Touch each cornea in turn. If touching the right cornea makes neither eye blink but touching the left makes both blink, the right trigeminal (afferent) side is at fault. If the right eye never blinks whichever side is touched, the right facial nerve (efferent) is at fault.

check.q: Name the afferent and efferent nerves of the corneal reflex.
check.a: Afferent: ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1). Efferent: facial nerve (VII) to orbicularis oculi.

steps.title: The plantar reflex
steps.text: Firmly stroke the lateral side of the sole with a blunt object, from the heel toward the ball of the foot and across under the toes. In a healthy adult the toes curl downward: a flexor plantar response. It is a polysynaptic reflex carried by the tibial nerve, and it needs the corticospinal (pyramidal) tracts to be working normally.

check.q: What is the normal adult response to stroking the lateral sole?
check.a: The toes flex (curl) - a flexor plantar response.

steps.title: The Babinski sign
steps.text:
In an extensor plantar response - the Babinski sign - the hallux (big toe) extends upward and the other toes fan out.

It is normal in infants under about 1 year, because their corticospinal tracts are not yet fully myelinated. In an adult it means damage to the pyramidal (corticospinal) tracts anywhere from the motor cortex down the spinal cord.
focus: Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot
steps.pitfall: An upgoing big toe is not 'a positive Babinski reflex' in the sense of a working reflex - it is an abnormal sign in adults. The normal adult reply is flexion.

check.q: Why is a Babinski sign normal in a 6-month-old but abnormal in an adult?
check.a: In infants the corticospinal tracts are incompletely myelinated; in adults the sign means those tracts are damaged.

practice.structure: Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot

practice.q: The afferent limb of the corneal reflex is the
choices: ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve
practice.why: V1 supplies sensation to the cornea; VII closes the lids.

practice.q: Which reflex CANNOT be voluntarily inhibited?
practice.why: The menace blink can be partly suppressed; the corneal reflex cannot.

practice.q: In an adult, stroking the lateral sole makes the big toe extend and the toes fan. This suggests
practice.why: The Babinski sign is an upper motor neuron sign in adults.

practice.q: How is the plantar reflex elicited?
practice.a: Stroke the lateral sole firmly from the heel toward the ball of the foot and across under the toes.

practice.q: Up to what age is an extensor plantar response normal, and why?
practice.a: About 1 year - until the corticospinal tracts are fully myelinated.

title: Skin receptors, touch and temperature

course.unit: Lab 1 · Nerve physiology, reflexes & general senses

summary: The receptors of the skin, why a fingertip feels two points where the back feels one, and why receptors adapt.
objectives: Name each cutaneous receptor, its depth in the skin, what it senses and how fast it adapts
Explain two-point discrimination with receptor density, receptive fields and the sensory homunculus
Describe cold and warm spots and why temperature perception is relative
Distinguish tonic from phasic receptors
takeaways: Meissner corpuscles (dermal papillae): light touch, rapidly adapting. Merkel discs (base of epidermis): light touch, slowly adapting.
Pacinian corpuscles (deep dermis and hypodermis): deep pressure and vibration. Free nerve endings: pain and temperature.
Small, dense receptive fields and a large cortical area give the fingertip a two-point threshold of ~2-5 mm; the back needs several centimetres.
Cold spots outnumber warm spots; thermoreceptors adapt, so temperature is judged relative to what the skin is used to.
Phasic receptors adapt quickly (touch, Meissner, Pacinian); tonic receptors keep firing (proprioceptors, pain).

steps.title: Touch receptors in the skin
steps.text:
Meissner (tactile) corpuscles sit in the dermal papillae just under the epidermis and signal light touch. Merkel discs (tactile discs) lie at the base of the epidermis and also sense light touch and texture. Pacinian (lamellated) corpuscles - onion-like layers around one nerve ending - sit deep in the dermis and hypodermis and sense deep pressure and vibration.

Thick skin of the fingertips and palm is packed with touch receptors.
focus: Distal phalanx of second finger of hand

check.q: Which receptor sits in the dermal papillae, and which deep in the dermis?
check.a: Meissner corpuscles in the dermal papillae; Pacinian corpuscles deep in the dermis and hypodermis.

steps.title: Pain and temperature: free nerve endings
steps.text:
Free (naked) nerve endings branch up into the epidermis. Many are nociceptors (pain receptors); others are thermoreceptors. Cold receptors and warm receptors both fire at a comfortable skin temperature; cooling speeds up the cold ones and warming the warm ones. Extreme heat or cold recruits nociceptors, so it hurts.

Probing the skin reveals separate cold spots and warm spots; cold spots are far more numerous.

check.q: Which are more numerous in the skin, cold spots or warm spots?
check.a: Cold spots.

steps.title: Two-point discrimination
steps.text:
Touch the skin with two points at once and narrow the gap until they feel like one: that distance is the two-point discrimination threshold, measured with an aesthesiometer (two-point discriminator). It is about 2-5 mm on a fingertip, larger on the palm, and several centimetres on the posterior forearm, arm, neck and back.

The reason is receptor density: where receptors are dense, each has a small receptive field, so two nearby points hit different receptors.
focus: Distal phalanx of second finger of hand

check.q: Why can a fingertip tell two points 3 mm apart when the back cannot?
check.a: Fingertip receptors are dense with small receptive fields, so the points stimulate separate receptors; on the back one large field covers both.

steps.title: Mapping and locating touch
steps.text:
A fine bristle or von Frey hair pressed on the skin shows sensitivity is punctate: some spots feel it, others between them do not. Tactile localisation - pointing, eyes closed, to where you were touched - is most accurate on the fingertip.

The brain matches this: in the postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex) the fingertips, lips and tongue occupy a huge share of the map, the sensory homunculus, while the back gets little.

check.q: Where is the sensory homunculus, and which body parts are largest on it?
check.a: In the postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex); the fingertips, lips and tongue.

steps.title: Adaptation: phasic and tonic receptors
steps.text:
A steady stimulus fades from awareness - clothes stop being felt within minutes. This sensory adaptation filters out unimportant, unchanging input. Phasic receptors adapt quickly and signal change: light touch, Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles. Tonic receptors keep firing: proprioceptors and pain receptors, whose message stays important.

Thermoreceptors adapt too, so temperature is judged relative to what the skin is used to: after cold water, room-temperature water feels warm; after warm water, the same water feels cool.

check.q: One hand has been in cold water, the other in warm. Both go into room-temperature water. What does each feel?
check.a: The cold-adapted hand feels warmth; the warm-adapted hand feels cool - perception is relative, not absolute.

practice.structure: Distal phalanx of second finger of hand

practice.q: Deep pressure and vibration are sensed mainly by
practice.why: Lamellated corpuscles lie deep in the dermis and hypodermis.

practice.q: A slowly adapting light-touch receptor at the base of the epidermis is the
practice.why: Merkel discs keep signalling sustained touch; Meissner corpuscles adapt rapidly.

practice.q: Nociceptors are
practice.why: Pain receptors are naked nerve endings.

practice.q: Where is the two-point threshold smallest?
practice.why: Highest receptor density and smallest receptive fields.

practice.q: A receptor that keeps firing during a sustained stimulus is
practice.why: Tonic receptors (e.g. proprioceptors, pain) adapt slowly.

practice.q: What is a receptive field?
practice.a: The area of skin in which a stimulus changes the firing of one sensory neuron.

practice.q: What does a von Frey hair show about touch sensitivity?
practice.a: That it is punctate - touch is felt at discrete spots over receptors, not evenly everywhere.

practice.q: What happens to thermoreceptors and pain receptors at extreme temperatures?
practice.a: Extreme heat or cold activates nociceptors, so the sensation becomes pain.

title: Proprioception, referred and projected pain

course.unit: Lab 1 · Nerve physiology, reflexes & general senses

summary: Knowing where your limbs are with your eyes shut, and why a sick organ hurts somewhere else.
objectives: Define proprioception and name its receptors
Explain referred pain by convergence of visceral and somatic afferents
Give the referred pain site for the heart, lungs and diaphragm, oesophagus, stomach, liver and gallbladder, colon, appendix, kidney, ureter and bladder
Explain projected sensation from the ulnar nerve at the elbow
takeaways: Proprioception, the sense of body and limb position, comes from muscle spindles, tendon organs and joint receptors.
Referred pain: visceral and skin afferents converge on the same spinal segments, and the brain blames the skin.
Heart -> left chest, left shoulder, medial left arm. Lungs and diaphragm -> base of neck and shoulder. Oesophagus -> behind the sternum.
Stomach -> epigastrium. Liver and gallbladder -> right shoulder and right upper abdomen. Colon -> periumbilical/lower abdomen. Appendix -> periumbilical, then right lower quadrant.
Kidney -> flank and lower back; ureter -> flank to groin; bladder -> suprapubic. Irritating the ulnar nerve at the elbow is felt in the little finger.

steps.title: Proprioception
steps.text:
Proprioception is the sense of where your body and limbs are, without looking. Its proprioceptors are muscle spindles (muscle length), tendon organs (tension) and joint receptors (joint angle). They are tonic: they keep reporting.

With your eyes closed you can still touch the lateral corner of your eye, your earlobe or your chin accurately - proprioception is guiding the hand.

check.q: Name three kinds of proprioceptor.
check.a: Muscle spindles, tendon organs and joint receptors.

steps.title: Why pain is referred
steps.text:
Pain receptors (nociceptors) in the viscera are free nerve endings, but visceral afferents enter the cord at the same segments as nerves from particular areas of skin, and converge on the same spinal neurons and pathways. The brain, used to pain from skin, blames the skin. The result is referred pain: visceral pain felt at a surface site.

The heart is the classic case. Angina pectoris and a heart attack (myocardial infarction) are felt in the left chest, left shoulder and medial left arm.

check.q: Why is cardiac pain felt in the left arm?
check.a: Cardiac afferents and afferents from the left arm and chest skin enter the same upper thoracic segments and converge on the same neurons, so the brain misattributes the pain.

steps.title: Chest and upper abdomen
steps.text: Lungs and diaphragm: the base of the neck and the shoulder (the diaphragm is supplied from C3-C5). Oesophagus: behind the sternum (substernal). Stomach: the epigastric region. Liver and gallbladder: the right upper abdomen and the right shoulder or scapula.

check.q: Gallbladder inflammation may be felt in which shoulder?
check.a: The right shoulder (or right scapula), together with the right upper abdomen.

steps.title: Lower abdomen and urinary tract
steps.text: Colon: around the umbilicus and the lower abdomen. Appendix: at first around the umbilicus, then, once the overlying peritoneum is inflamed, the right lower quadrant. Kidney: the flank and lower back (lumbar region). Ureter: from the flank down to the groin. Urinary bladder: above the pubis (suprapubic).
steps.clinical: Appendicitis classically starts as vague periumbilical pain (visceral, referred) and moves to the right iliac fossa when the parietal peritoneum becomes involved.

check.q: Where is pain from a stone in the ureter felt?
check.a: In the flank, radiating down to the groin.

steps.title: Projected sensation: the 'funny bone'
steps.text: A nerve stimulated anywhere along its course is felt where its endings are. Knock the ulnar nerve behind the medial elbow, or rest the elbow in ice water, and you feel tingling and aching in the little finger and the ulnar side of the hand - not at the elbow. This projected sensation shows the brain always maps a nerve's signals to its receptive territory.
steps.pitfall: Projected sensation is not referred pain: it comes from stimulating a nerve trunk itself, not from convergence of visceral and skin afferents.

check.q: Your elbow rests in ice water. Where do you feel tingling, and which nerve is responsible?
check.a: In the little finger and ulnar side of the hand - the ulnar nerve, stimulated at the elbow.

practice.q: Pain from angina pectoris is typically referred to the
choices: left chest, shoulder and medial arm
practice.why: Cardiac afferents share upper thoracic segments with the left chest and arm.

practice.q: Early appendicitis pain is usually felt
practice.why: It later moves to the right lower quadrant.

practice.q: Referred pain from the kidney is felt in the
practice.why: Renal afferents enter the lower thoracic and upper lumbar segments.

practice.q: Referred pain from the lungs and diaphragm is felt at the
choices: base of the neck and shoulder
practice.why: The diaphragm's sensory supply shares C3-C5 with the neck and shoulder.

practice.q: Define proprioception.
practice.a: The sense of the position and movement of the body and limbs, from muscle spindles, tendon organs and joint receptors.

practice.q: Where is referred pain from the oesophagus, the stomach and the urinary bladder felt?
practice.a: Oesophagus: behind the sternum. Stomach: epigastrium. Bladder: suprapubic.

practice.q: How does referred pain differ from projected sensation?
practice.a: Referred pain comes from viscera via converging afferents; projected sensation comes from stimulating a nerve trunk and is felt in that nerve's territory.
